stem.text: The function f gives the height, in meters, of a drone above the ground at time x seconds. The function f is continuous for all real x and differentiable for all x except \( x = \frac{11}{2} \), where its graph has a corner. Selected values of f are given in the table. Does the Mean Value Theorem guarantee a value c, with \( 3 < c < 8 \), such that \( f'(c) = \frac{1}{5} \)? Justify the answer.

answer_key.label: No. Although \( \frac{f(8) - f(3)}{8 - 3} = \frac{1}{5} \), f is not differentiable at \( x = \frac{11}{2} \), which lies in \( (3, 8) \), so the Mean Value Theorem does not apply and such a c is not guaranteed.

worked_solution.text: The average rate of change of f over \( \left[3, 8\right] \) is \( \frac{f(8) - f(3)}{8 - 3} = \frac{3 - 2}{5} = \frac{1}{5} \).

The Mean Value Theorem needs f continuous on \( \left[3, 8\right] \) and differentiable on \( (3, 8) \), but f is not differentiable at \( x = \frac{11}{2} \), which lies in \( (3, 8) \). The theorem does not apply, and no other fact given forces \( f'(c) = \frac{1}{5} \) anywhere in the interval, so the answer is no.
worked_solution.rule_named: hypotheses of the Mean Value Theorem

options.label: Yes. Since \( \frac{f(8) - f(3)}{8 - 3} = \frac{1}{5} \), the Mean Value Theorem guarantees such a c, with f taken to be differentiable on \( (3, 8) \).
options.derivation: the Mean Value Theorem applied without checking its hypotheses, which fail at x = 11/2

options.label: Yes. Since \( \frac{f(8) - f(3)}{8 - 3} = \frac{1}{5} \), there is a c with \( 3 < c < 8 \) and \( f'(c) = \frac{1}{5} \), because an average rate of change is always reached by the derivative.
options.derivation: existence asserted from the arithmetic alone, with no theorem named and no check that one applies

options.label: No. Although \( \frac{f(8) - f(3)}{8 - 3} = \frac{1}{5} \), f is not differentiable at \( x = \frac{11}{2} \), which lies in \( (3, 8) \), so the Mean Value Theorem does not apply and such a c is not guaranteed.
Yes. Since \( \frac{f(8) - f(3)}{8 - 3} = \frac{1}{5} \), the Intermediate Value Theorem guarantees such a c, with f taken to be continuous on \( \left[3, 8\right] \).
options.derivation: the Intermediate Value Theorem cited for a claim about the derivative
